initial_presentation: The patient is a 5-year-old girl born at term via normal vaginal delivery after an uneventful pregnancy to a healthy mother, with no neonatal complications. She is fully vaccinated according to the Saudi national vaccine schedule, and there is no family history of medical or surgical diseases. Her developmental milestones were achieved at the expected times.

A 22-year-old male presented with a rash and joint pain persisting for four months, along with breathlessness for one month. Five months prior to admission, he had a butterfly tattoo on his right chest using blue and red ink. Four months before admission, erythema appeared on various skin areas, including the face, the extensor surface of both elbows, the metacarpophalangeal joints (MCP2–4), the neck, the chest, and the right side of the back. There was no muscle weakness reported. Over time, he experienced increasing shortness of breath following physical activity.

A 7-year-old girl with yellowish skin and eyes, the firstborn child of healthy parents (Korean father and Vietnamese mother) at 39 weeks of gestation, visited the Division of Endocrinology, Department of Pediatrics, Jeonbuk National University Hospital (Jeonju, South Korea), for evaluation of ongoing hemolytic anemia. Physical examination revealed chronic illness appearance, yellowish skin, yellowing of the sclera, enlarged liver, and enlarged spleen. The rest of the examination was normal. She was born at 38 weeks via vaginal delivery, with a birth weight of 2,300 g and an uneventful perinatal history. She was admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit after birth due to lethargy and received a transfusion of packed red cells. Over time, she developed paleness and progressively bright yellow skin discoloration. There was no family history of hemolytic disease.
A 10-year-old girl was admitted with a history of convulsion followed by unconsciousness since day one.

A 16-year-old male from Cape Town, South Africa, presented with dental pain due to a severely decayed tooth. He is the only child of parents who are not related by blood and has no notable family medical history. His medical history includes gastrointestinal and eye issues, which are currently being managed. He experiences progressive vision blurring, eye itching, and dryness. He also has recurring episodes of diarrhea, abdominal cramps, constipation, and allergic rhinitis. He shows signs of mouth-breathing and has a vertical maxillary excess with an excessively gummy smile. His dental examination revealed a Class III malocclusion with a protrusive lower jaw and prominent chin. He has prominent ears and thick, arched eyebrows. Both his upper and lower jaw ridges are bulbous, with the upper ridge being more affected, especially on the palatal side, creating a narrow, deep palate appearance. His gums are pale, thick, and smooth with mild pigmentation on the attached gums of the lower jaw. The upper central incisors have not erupted. The visible teeth are severely worn, small, and spaced apart. The lower incisors are barrel-shaped, and the only erupted permanent molar is also severely decayed. The erupted teeth have smooth enamel surfaces.

A 25-year-old woman reported experiencing persistent shoulder pain since her teenage years. Over the years, she had tried various treatments including different non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), local steroid injections, and physiotherapy. The pain was described as diffuse, vague, and chronic, without significantly limiting her range of motion. It was more intense at night, leading to multiple episodes of sleep disruption. Physical examination revealed notable tenderness on the clavicle.

A 41-year-old woman presented to the ER with a 4-week history of dizziness, nausea, and vomiting. She had a past medical history of antiphospholipid syndrome associated with spontaneous abortions but was otherwise in good health.

A 2-month-old male presented with a 3-day history of cough, 2 days of rapid breathing and poor feeding, and 1 day of fever. He had intermittent fever starting from day 4 of life, accompanied by a dry, non-paroxysmal cough. The antenatal and birth history were normal, with a birth weight of 3000 g, and he was discharged on day 2 of life. During the first week, he exhibited a weak cry and reduced spontaneous movement in all four limbs. Developmentally, he did not achieve neck holding but showed regard for his mother's face, responded to sound, and followed objects. The family history revealed that he was the third child in a non-consanguineous marriage, with two male siblings who had early infantile deaths at 50 and 90 days, respectively, following a history of hypotonia. On examination, he had a heart rate of 143/min, respiratory rate of 68/min, and oxygen saturation of 50% on room air. His weight was 3.6 kg (-3 Z score), length 58 cm (0.88 Z score), and occipitofrontal circumference 36.2 cm (-2.5 Z score). Muscle weakness was noted with a frog-like posture, jug-handle deformity of the upper limbs, bilateral wrist contracture, bell-shaped chest, and poor spontaneous activity. He was awake and alert with spontaneous eye-opening, extra-ocular movements, and no ptosis or facial weakness. Tongue fasciculations and flabby skeletal muscles were present. Hypotonia was indicated by head lag when pulled to sit, dangling legs on ventral suspension, and head lying below the plane of the body on horizontal suspension. There were minimal spontaneous distal movements and no antigravity movements. Deep tendon reflexes were absent, and bilateral plantar responses were mute. Sensations were intact, and there was no nystagmus. Respiratory examination showed nasal flaring, bell-shaped chest, bilateral suprasternal, intercostal, and subcostal retractions with a seesaw breathing pattern, indicating intercostal muscle weakness. Chest auscultation revealed decreased air entry with bilateral crackles.
A 56-year-old woman presented with epigastric pain and an enlarged liver approximately 15 years prior to the development of a hepatic tumor.

A 43-year-old male reported experiencing excessive thirst and urination for six months. His daily urine output ranged from 3.5 to 6 liters, with a urine specific gravity of 1.003 (normal range: 1.010–1.025).
